title: Iron smelting at Meroe
summary: Iron was smelted at Meroe on the Nile in Sudan from at least the seventh to sixth century BCE, and the practice lasted over a thousand years. Large heaps of slag and furnace debris mark the city as one of the largest ironmaking centres in Africa. A Penn Museum article dates slag from a deep level to the 6th century BCE.

uncertainty.note: UCL researchers say new radiocarbon dates suggest significant-scale iron production from at least the seventh–sixth century B.C. and for over one thousand years. The Penn Museum article reports "MR-7 514 ± 73 B.C." for slag at Level 16. The end year is the start plus the stated "over one thousand years", a minimum.

as_recorded.value: from at least the seventh - sixth century B.C., and was practiced at the site for over one thousand years

when.display: From the 7th–6th century BCE, for over 1,000 years

where.historical_name: Royal city of Meroe, Kingdom of Kush

importance.justification: The Penn Museum article calls the Level 16 slag date the oldest for iron working obtained in sub-Saharan Africa.

sources.title: Iron Smelting in Sudan: Experimental Archaeology at the Royal City of Meroe
sources.publisher: University College London (Journal of Field Archaeology)
sources.author: Humphris et al.

reviewer_note: Dates differ by source: UCL gives 7th–6th century BCE (2017 radiocarbon), Penn (1993) a single 6th-century date; I set start at -600 (601 BCE) as the 6th/7th century boundary. The end year is a floor derived from "over one thousand years". Placed under northern_africa (UN M49 treats Sudan so) though Penn says sub-Saharan. UCL says no furnace earlier than the first century AD has yet been found at Meroe, which I did not put in the summary.
